Chapter 30

Remote functions

query, command and form from $app/server — what replaces most of an API, and the one job left for a real endpoint.

By the end of this chapter

Call the server as if it were a function, with validation, CSRF and types for free.

Tessera has exactly two API routes. Everything else that would have been an endpoint is a remote function: an async function you export from a .remote.ts file and *import into a component*, where calling it performs a typed, validated, CSRF-protected request.

Three things without any code: the payload is validated by the same valibot schema the client imports, the CSRF origin check runs, and the call is typed end to end — so a change to PushSchema breaks the caller at build time rather than at runtime in production.

A refusal is data, not a crash

The client has already applied these operations locally — that is what local-first means — so it needs a status it can *act on*. 403 means "stop and reload". 422 means "your clock is wrong and this will keep happening". A 500 would tell it to retry forever, which for a permanent failure is a client that hammers the server until the tab closes. The IngestError → error(status, message) translation is three lines and it is what makes #onPushFailure in chapter 23 able to distinguish retryable from not.

query

Note how little it does. It reads a row and returns it. It does not replay operations, build a document, or hold a CRDT in memory — the client streams everything after that sequence and applies it itself, which it has to be able to do anyway because that is the same path every subsequent edit takes.

The alternative — a server that materialises the current state on every open — looks tidier and gives the server an opinion about the document, which then has to agree with the client’s opinion forever. When two authorities disagree about a CRDT, the one with the database usually wins, and the user’s unsynced work is what loses.

Awaiting the board, and what a boundary is handed

The page learns which board to open from its props, not from a global. SvelteKit generates a $types module beside every route, and its PageProps types both things a page is given: data, from the load functions above it, and params, from the URL — for this route, { lang?: Locale; board: string }.

This page used to read page.params.board! from $app/state. The global page is typed for every route at once, so board is string | undefined there, and calling anything with it took a ! — an assertion that can be wrong, about a value this route already guarantees. The props are typed for *this* route. A hand-written interface Props { data: PageData } is the older spelling of half the same thing: the documentation marks it legacy, “before 2.16.0”, and every route component in Tessera now takes PageProps or LayoutProps instead.

Then the query: derived from that parameter in the script, and awaited in the markup, inside a <svelte:boundary>.

Why $derived

SvelteKit reuses a page component when the URL changes but the route does not: going from /boards/a to /boards/b keeps this instance and hands it new params. A query called once — const board = openBoard(params.board) — would go on showing board a. $derived re-runs the call when params.board changes, and the compiler agrees: a plain const that reads a prop earns a warning that it “only captures the initial value”. It is the documentation’s own idiom for a query with an argument — let { params } = $props(); const post = $derived(await getPost(params.slug)); — with one difference, explained next: the await here is in the markup rather than the script.

The await lives in the markup because of where its boundary is. An await in the *script* suspends the whole component, so the boundary in its own markup could not catch it; the wait and the failure would belong to whatever is above. Awaited inside the page’s own <svelte:boundary>, it gives that boundary both of its jobs: until the promise resolves it shows its pending snippet, and if the promise rejects it shows its failed snippet instead. In the documentation’s words, “until the promise resolves — and if it errors — the nearest <svelte:boundary> will be invoked.”

{const caught = $derived(error as App.Error)} is a declaration tag: a const (or let) written in markup, which names a value for everything after it in the same scope. Since Svelte 5.56 it is how markup declares a value, and the older {@const} tag is, in the documentation’s words, “considered legacy — use declaration tags instead.” The $derived is not decoration. A bare {const} is evaluated once, when the tag is reached, and the documentation’s rule is that “when values should be reactive, you can use $state and $derived” — which is what keeps caught in step with the error it reads. Chapter 31 uses one to name an awaited list, and chapter 36 one inside an {#each}, where its scope matters.

Why await, and not .current

A query also has current, loading and error properties, and current looks like the simpler thing to read: {#if board.current}<Workspace … />{/if}. That is what this page first did, and a board that did not exist rendered as an empty screen. .current never throws. A query that fails leaves it undefined and puts the error on .error, so nothing inside the boundary ever fails and its failed snippet never runs — the person sees a blank page and nothing is logged anywhere. await is what hands the rejection to the boundary.

What arrives in failed is worth knowing exactly, because it is not the value that was thrown. SvelteKit passes everything a boundary catches through the handleError hook first, so the snippet receives an App.Error: { status, message }, plus whatever fields you declared in app.d.ts — here the correlation id. The server’s error(404, 'No such board.') arrives as { status: 404, message: 'No such board.' }. A plain exception thrown while rendering arrives as whatever hooks.client.ts made of it — “Something went wrong in the browser. Your board is safe on this device.” Either way the text is its message. String(error), which is what this snippet first printed, gives [object Object].

The documentation writes the snippet as failed(error: App.Error). Under this project’s strict settings svelte-check rejects that annotation: Svelte types the parameter as unknown, because it cannot know what SvelteKit’s transformError returns, and a snippet that only accepts an App.Error is not assignable to one that must accept anything. So the parameter stays untyped and the value is cast where it is read. The cast says out loud what the type system cannot know, and the end-to-end test below is what keeps it honest.

The other shape: a command that says no

A command, or a form submission you await yourself, fails differently. It never goes near a boundary: it rejects, at the await, with an HttpError — { status, body }, where body is the App.Error. An HttpError is not an Error, so it has no message of its own. The server’s words are body.message, and isHttpError from @sveltejs/kit is the type guard that lets TypeScript see it.

  • A boundary’s failed snippet or onerror handler, a query’s .error, and page.error on an error page: an App.Error. Read error.message.
  • An awaited command(), or form.submit() inside enhance: an HttpError. Read thrown.body.message.
  • A form() spread without enhance that fails: SvelteKit renders the nearest +error.svelte, where page.error is an App.Error again.

Mixing them up fails quietly in both directions. error.body.message in a failed snippet throws inside the snippet; thrown.message in a catch is undefined, and the line meant to explain the refusal is blank. Chapter 36 has the second case, where a viewer presses a button the server will refuse — and chapter 23’s #onPushFailure reads the same shape through the same isHttpError guard, for exactly this reason.

One status never reaches this boundary: 401. openBoard would answer it for a visitor who is not signed in, and a heading over “Sign in to continue.” with nothing to click is a dead end — on the one URL in the app that people paste into chat. So the route has a server load whose only job is to send a signed-out visitor to the sign-in page, with from set so they come straight back:

Returning something with behaviour

openBoard returns a LoadedBoard, which is a *class*. That works because of the transport hook, and it is worth seeing what it buys.

Read the warning at the top of that block before adding an entry of your own. SvelteKit serialises with devalue, which already handles Date, Map, Set, RegExp, BigInt, URL, Infinity, NaN, -0 and cyclic references. Most reaching for transport is unnecessary, and every unnecessary entry is a pair of functions that can drift apart. Both entries here carry behaviour, which is the thing devalue genuinely cannot reconstruct.

The payoff: the browser gets an object that can hydrate() itself into a reactive document. The alternative is every call site doing BoardDocument.fromSnapshot(actorId(), result.snapshot) and one of them eventually forgetting the actor — which, per chapter 21, is a bug that presents as typing occasionally vanishing.

What is left for a real endpoint

  • /api/boards/[board]/stream — a GET that never ends. A remote function returns a value; this returns a ReadableStream that stays open for hours.
  • /api/boards/[board]/snapshot — a document, fetched by an embedded custom element on somebody else’s page, which has no SvelteKit client to call a remote function with.

That is a useful rule of thumb for the whole feature: a remote function replaces a request/response endpoint. It does not replace a stream or a public document.

Checkpoint

  • You can call the server from a component with no fetch, no route and no manual types.
  • Changing a schema breaks the caller at build time.
  • A board that does not exist says “No such board.” rather than showing an empty page.
  • The board page reads its id from PageProps’ typed params, with no !, and derives its query from it.
  • A signed-out visitor who opens a board link is sent to sign in, and then back to the board.
  • You can say which of the two error shapes a failed snippet gets, and which one a catch gets.
  • You can name the two things a remote function is not for.
